title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
gist: *sshole is a decade-old flaw in how OpenSSH interacts with musl on non-PAM systems such as Alpine Linux. It lets attackers log into passwordless ('*') accounts with a single connection by entering more than 256 characters. It likely affects many containers and embedded devices that are hard to patch (the Alpine Docker image has over 1 billion downloads), and has no CVE yet.

insights.claim: A decade-old vulnerability called *sshole lets attackers log into some Alpine Linux systems without a password because of an interaction between OpenSSH and the musl libc library when PAM is not used.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A long-hidden auth bypass in core open-source infrastructure shows supply-chain risk for container-heavy enterprises.
insights.quote: “An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,”
insights.locator: When all the conditions are met

insights.claim: Exploiting *sshole requires an active account with a SHA256 or SHA512 password hash, whose salt sshd borrows, and a target account marked passwordless with '*' in /etc/shadow; the attacker enters more than 256 characters as the password.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The narrow preconditions limit exposure, but passwordless certificate-auth accounts are common.

insights.claim: Checkpoint reports root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting, but reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still escalate to root.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: An attacker can still get full control of a compromised system through privilege escalation.

insights.claim: *sshole likely threatens many systems because the Alpine Docker Hub base image has over 1 billion downloads and Alpine is common in routers, smart TVs, industrial controllers, and other embedded devices that often cannot be updated.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Vulnerable IoT and industrial devices that can't be patched will stay exposed for a long time, which supports demand for network-level security.

insights.claim: Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and although only a fraction are vulnerable to *sshole, the speed of testing each one makes finding targets easy.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Easy mass scanning makes it likely that opportunistic exploitation begins quickly.

themes.theme: Disputed responsibility between OpenSSH and musl

insights.claim: OpenSSH says the root cause of *sshole lies outside sshd, while musl developer Rich Felker says it is erroneous use by the caller rather than a musl bug; both OpenSSH and Alpine have issued updates, and no CVE has been assigned.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: With no CVE and each project blaming the other, vulnerability scanners may miss the flaw and patching may be slow.
insights.quote: “It is my position that this is not a bug in musl just an erroneous use by the caller.”

insights.claim: The discoverer of *sshole says OpenWRT, buildroot, and yocto are affected, though OpenWRT uses Dropbear by default and the buildroot and yocto claims are unconfirmed.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: If confirmed, many more embedded firmware stacks would be exposed.
insights.locator: It’s not yet known what other
